neighbours.label: In a description of a named microcontroller chip or board (AVR, STM32, Arduino-style), the list of its built-in parts and interfaces (timers, serial ports, ADC, PWM pins), peaking on the count word or article just before a part. Quiet for microcontroller talk that lists no parts, and for parts lists of other devices (amplifiers, meters, kitchens, cars). Gym-class and running-gear text also fires, but patchily.
neighbours.notes: Step-in reader of bonsai1/L31/N9952+ (drop 0.37). Cold run: labelled from own tops and probes only. Probes: chip peripheral lists 0.33-0.89; chip talk without parts ~0.03; amplifier/oscilloscope/kitchen/car lists <=0.12; gym-class text 0.08-0.84 (HIIT/CrossFit with bracketed expansion highest); acronym expansions outside fitness quiet. Solver leak: running-sock and fitness-class text. Test written blind from the label only.
fire: The ATmega328P includes three timers, one USART, a 10-bit ADC with six channels, and six PWM pins.
The STM32F103 offers two SPI interfaces, two I2C buses, three USARTs and a 12-bit ADC.
On the Arduino Uno you get 14 digital I/O pins, six analog inputs, a serial port and a 16 MHz crystal.
The ATtiny85 packs two 8-bit timers, a four-channel ADC, and a universal serial interface into an eight-pin package.
Our board uses an STM32F4 with a CAN controller, four general-purpose timers, an RTC and a USB OTG port.
The Arduino Mega 2560 has 54 digital pins, of which 15 can be used as PWM outputs, plus 16 analog inputs and four hardware UARTs.
The ESP32 chip integrates two cores, a Wi-Fi radio, 18 ADC channels, two DACs and three UART interfaces.
Peripherals on the ATmega2560 include six timers, a watchdog timer, an analog comparator and an SPI port.
quiet: - 59 Seconds: Think a Little, Change a Lot, by Richard Wiseman
The ATmega328P is a popular chip that many hobbyists learn on before moving to bigger projects.
I flashed new firmware onto the STM32F103 last night and it finally booted without errors.
The Arduino Uno was the first board I ever bought, and it still sits on my desk today.
The ATtiny85 is cheap and small, which makes it ideal for little blinking toys.
Our team switched to an STM32F4 because the vendor's documentation was easier to follow.
This stereo amplifier has two input channels, a phono stage, a headphone jack and four speaker terminals.
